column1: l1/guten-morgen|Good morning!|Good morning, Ms Lange!|Used in the morning, until about 10–11 a.m.
l1/guten-tag|Hello! / Good day! (polite)|Hello, Mr Becker!|The most common polite greeting, roughly 11 a.m.–6 p.m. A final g sounds like k: Tag → "Tak".
l1/guten-abend|Good evening!|Good evening, ladies and gentlemen!|From about 6 p.m. A final d sounds like t: Abend → "Abent".
l1/gute-nacht|Good night!|Good night, Mum!|Only said when parting late at night or before going to bed — never as a greeting.
l1/hallo|Hi! / Hello! (informal)|Hi, Tom!|Fine at any time of day with friends and people you know.
l1/tschuess|Bye! (informal)|Bye, Anna!|Also spelt Tschüss. Use it with friends and people you know.
l1/auf-wiedersehen|Goodbye! (polite)|Goodbye, Mr Becker!|Literally "until we see again". Use with strangers, in shops and offices.
l1/bis-spaeter|See you later!|Bye, see you later!|sp at the start of a word sounds like "shp": später → "shpäter".
l1/willkommen|Welcome!|Welcome to Berlin!|willkommen = welcome; herzlich = warmly (can be left out).
l1/danke|thank you, thanks|Thank you, Ms Lange!|
l1/frau|Ms, Mrs (+ surname); woman|Hello, Ms Lange!|Frau + SURNAME: Frau Lange. Used for every adult woman.
l1/herr|Mr (+ surname); gentleman|Good evening, Mr Becker!|Herr + SURNAME: Herr Becker.
l1/dame|lady|Ladies and gentlemen, welcome!|Common in: meine Damen und Herren = ladies and gentlemen.
l1/ich|I|I am Mai.|ch after i is soft, like a whispered "h" in "huge" — not "ick".
l1/sie-hoeflich|you (polite)|And you?|Always written with a capital S. Verbs with Sie end in -en.
l1/heissen|to be called|My name is Linh.|
l1/sein|to be|I am Minh.|Irregular verb — learn it by heart.
l1/name|name|My name is Lan.|Ends in -e but takes der — remember the blue colour!
l1/wie|how; (asking a name) what|What's your name?|
l1/das-ist|This is … (introducing someone)|This is Mr Becker.|
l1/entschuldigung|Excuse me! (to ask or call someone); apology|Excuse me, what is your name?|Nouns ending in -ung are always die.
l1/freut-mich|Nice to meet you!||eu sounds like "oy": freut → "froyt".
l1/ja|yes||j sounds like the English y in "yes".
l1/ich-weiss-es-nicht|I don't know.||weiß is a form of the verb wissen (to know).
l1/sprechen|to speak|I speak Vietnamese.|With du the e changes to i: du sprichst.
l1/und|and|I speak Vietnamese and English.|A final d sounds like t: "unt".
l1/ein-bisschen|a little, a bit|I speak a little German.|
l1/firma|company, firm|I'm from the company Sonntag.|
l1/von|from; of||v usually sounds like f: von → "fon".
l1/schweiz|Switzerland||Takes an article: die Schweiz → aus der Schweiz.
l1/vietnam|Vietnam||A foreign name, so the v here sounds like v.
l1/deutsch|German (language)||Language names are always capitalised: Ich spreche Deutsch.
l1/tuerkei|Turkey||Takes an article: die Türkei → aus der Türkei.
l1/usa|USA||Plural: die USA → aus den USA.
l1/buchstabe|letter (of the alphabet)||Ends in -e but takes der.
l1/bitte|please; here you are|One moment, please.|
l1/ich-buchstabiere|I'll spell it: …|I'll spell it: P – H – A – M.|
l1/vielen-dank|Thank you very much!||v sounds like f: vielen → "feelen".
l1/ist-da|Is … there?|Is Mr Krause there, please?|da sein = to be there, to be present.
l1/auf-wiederhoeren|Goodbye! (on the phone)||hören = to hear → "until we hear again". Only used on the phone.
l1/vorname|first name||Nguyễn Văn An → Vorname: An (or Van An).
l1/familienname|surname, family name||Also called Nachname. Nguyễn Văn An → Familienname: Nguyen.
l1/strasse|street, road||In Switzerland it is spelt Strasse (no ß).
l1/postleitzahl|postcode, ZIP code||Short form: PLZ. In Germany it has 5 digits, e.g. 80331 München.
l1/stadt|city, town||st at the start sounds like "sht", dt like t: "Shtatt".
l1/k-ansehen|Look at the photos.||ansehen = to look at; the "an" moves to the end of the sentence.
l1/k-ankreuzen|Tick / mark with a cross.||ankreuzen = to mark with a cross.
l2/wie-gehts|How are you? / How's it going?|Hi, Tim! How's it going?|geht's = geht es. The h in "geht" is silent and just makes the vowel long: "gayt".
l2/wie-geht-es-dir|How are you? (informal)||dir is the form of du used after "geht es".
l2/wie-geht-es-ihnen|How are you? (polite)||Ihnen is the form of Sie; the I is always capital.
l2/super|great, super|Thanks, great!|s before a vowel is voiced like "z": "zooper".
l2/sehr|very|That is very good!|The h is silent and lengthens the e; a final r is soft like "a": "zay-a".
l2/na-ja|well…; so-so|Well, it's OK.|Often comes before "es geht" when you are not really happy.
l2/nicht-so-gut|Not so good.|Oh, not so good.|
l2/ach|oh, ah||ch after a is a throaty sound, as in Scottish "loch" (Nacht, auch).
l2/lernen|to learn, to study|I'm learning German.|lernen = to learn a subject, a skill, a language.
l2/haben|to have|We have a break.|Irregular: du hast, er/sie hat (the b drops out).
l2/lehrerin|teacher (female)|Ms Lange is a teacher.|Add -in to a male job title to get the female form: Lehrer → Lehrerin.
l2/familie|family|This is my family.|The ending is said in two syllables "-lee-eh": fa-MEE-lee-eh.
l2/eltern|parents|These are my parents.|Plural only: die Eltern = mother and father.
l2/vater|father|My father is a teacher.|Long a; the plural has ä: Väter.
l2/mutter|mother|My mother's name is Anna.|Short u (double t); the plural has ü: Mütter.
l2/grosseltern|grandparents|These are my grandparents.|Groß- = big, grand. Plural only.
l2/grossvater|grandfather||German has no separate words for paternal and maternal grandparents.
l2/bruder|brother|This is my brother.|Long u; the plural has ü: Brüder.
l2/schwester|sister|This is my sister.|schw sounds like "shv".
l2/geschwister|siblings, brothers and sisters|These are my siblings.|One word for brothers and sisters together. Plural only.
l2/sohn|son|This is my son.|Long o (because of h); the plural has ö: Söhne.
l2/tochter|daughter|This is my daughter.|ch after o is throaty, short o; the plural has ö: Töchter.
l2/kind|child|This is my child.|Used for sons and daughters. A final d sounds like t.
l2/mann|husband; man|This is my husband.|mein Mann = my husband · meine Frau = my wife.
l2/ehefrau|wife (formal)||Ehe = marriage. Used on forms; in everyday speech: mein Mann, meine Frau.
l2/mein|my|This is my father.|mein + Bruder, Kind (der/das) · meine + Tochter, Kinder (die, plural).
l2/dein|your (informal)|Is that your sister?|Goes with du and follows the same rule as mein: dein Bruder · deine Mutter.
l2/ihr-art|your (polite)|Is that your son?|Goes with Sie and is always capitalised: Ihr Sohn · Ihre Tochter.
l2/das-sind|These are … (several people/things)|These are my parents.|Singular: Das ist … · Plural: Das sind …
l2/er|he, it (masculine)|This is Tim. He comes from Canada.|
l2/wir|we|We come from Vietnam.|w sounds like v: "veer".
l2/leben|to live|My parents live in Hanoi.|
l2/wohnen|to live (reside)|I live in Berlin.|wohnen is about where you live: Ich wohne in Köln. The h is silent.
l2/wo|where|Where do you live?|wo = where · woher = where from · wer = who.
l2/jetzt|now|Now I live in Cologne.|j = y, tz = ts: "yetst".
l2/hier|here|I live here.|ie = long ee; a final r is soft.
l2/aber|but|I come from Hanoi, but I live in Berlin.|
l2/schon|already|I've lived here for a long time.|Often with lange: schon lange = for a long time already.
l2/lange|long (time)||ng as in "sing", without a hard g.
l2/zurzeit|at the moment, currently|At the moment I live in Cologne.|
l2/n1|1 · one||When counting or saying phone numbers: eins. Before a noun it is ein / eine (ein Kind).
l2/n5|5 · five||ü: round your lips and say "ee".
l2/n7|7 · seven||s sounds like z, ie = long ee: "zee-ben".
l2/n8|8 · eight||ch after a is throaty.
l2/n10|10 · ten||z = ts; the h is silent.
l2/n11|11 · eleven||Special form — learn by heart.
l2/n12|12 · twelve||Special form. ö: round your lips and say "ay".
l2/n16|16 · sixteen||Drop the s: sech-zehn (not sechs-zehn).
l2/zahl|number, digit||z sounds like ts: "tsahl"; long a (because of h).
